definition: The difference in electrical potential between two points: the 'push' that drives current. It is always measured between two points, usually a point of interest and ground, in volts (V).
example: "This pin is at 3.3 V" means it is 3.3 V higher than the circuit's ground.

definition: The rate at which electric charge flows past a point, written I and measured in amperes (A). One ampere is one coulomb of charge per second. Current flows through a component, and it needs a complete loop to flow at all.
example: A 1 kΩ resistor with 5 V across it carries 5 mA.

definition: How strongly something opposes electric current, written R and measured in ohms (Ω). For a resistor it is the fixed ratio of voltage to current given by Ohm's law.
example: A resistor with 5 V across it and 2.5 mA through it has a resistance of 2 kΩ.

definition: The rate at which electrical energy is transferred or turned into heat or light, written P and measured in watts (W). For any part it is voltage times current.
example: A resistor with 3.3 V across it and 10 mA through it turns 33 mW into heat.

definition: The electrical power a component turns into heat. Every part has a limit; exceed it and the part overheats, drifts or fails.
example: A 100 Ω resistor across 5 V dissipates 0.25 W, the full rating of a typical small resistor.

definition: The SI unit of electric charge. One ampere of current moves one coulomb of charge past a point every second.
The SI unit of energy. One watt of power is one joule transferred every second.
The current flowing into any junction equals the current flowing out, because charge isn't created or lost. In a single loop this means the same current flows through every part.
example: If 10 mA flows through an LED's series resistor, 10 mA also flows through the LED.

definition: Around any closed loop, the voltage rises add up to the voltage drops. It is how you find the voltage left for one part once the others have taken theirs.
example: With a 5 V supply, 3.3 V across the resistor leaves 1.7 V across the LED.

definition: The conductive metal case or frame of a piece of equipment used as a reference or shield. Whether it is joined to circuit 0 V depends on the design.

The convention that current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal through the external circuit. Every formula, datasheet and schematic symbol uses it, even though in metal wires the moving charges are electrons drifting the other way.
example: In a forward-biased diode, conventional current flows from anode to cathode.

definition: A negatively charged particle. In metal wires electrons are the charge carriers, so they drift from − to +, opposite to conventional current; both descriptions give the same answers.

A letter in front of a unit that multiplies it by a power of ten: M (mega, 10⁶), k (kilo, 10³), m (milli, 10⁻³), µ (micro, 10⁻⁶), n (nano, 10⁻⁹), p (pico, 10⁻¹²). Case matters: m and M differ by a factor of 10⁹.
example: 100 nF is the same as 0.1 µF.

definition: The international metric system of units, including the volt, ampere, ohm, watt, farad and second, and the metric prefixes used to scale them.
The metric prefix meaning a million (10⁶). Note the capital M; a lower-case m means milli.
The metric prefix meaning a thousand (10³).
The metric prefix meaning one thousandth (10⁻³). Lower-case m; capital M means mega.
The metric prefix meaning one millionth (10⁻⁶), written with the Greek letter µ (mu) or, where that isn't available, a plain u.
The metric prefix meaning one billionth (10⁻⁹).
The metric prefix meaning one trillionth (10⁻¹²).
example: 1000 pF is 1 nF.

definition: One millionth of an ampere. Datasheets often specify input leakage and light-load output figures in microamps.
example: A logic output tested at 20 µA is under a very light load.

definition: One trillionth of a farad (10⁻¹² F). Small ceramic capacitors and stray capacitances are measured in picofarads.
example: The capacitor code 104 means 100,000 pF, which is 100 nF.

definition: A way of writing component values on schematics with the prefix letter (or R for ohms) in place of the decimal point, so a lost dot can't change the value. It is part of IEC 60062.
example: 4k7 means 4.7 kΩ, 2R2 means 2.2 Ω and 100n means 100 nF.

definition: An unbroken path from a supply's positive terminal, through the load and back to its negative terminal. Current flows only when the loop is complete; break it anywhere and the current everywhere in it stops.
A break in a circuit, or a path with effectively infinite resistance, so no current flows. A multimeter shows OL (or 1) when measuring resistance across an open circuit.
The conductor that carries current back to the source to complete the loop, usually ground. In audio cables the sleeve or shield is the signal's return path.
An adjustable mains-powered DC supply for testing circuits, usually with a voltage setting, a current limit and meters for both.
example: Set the current limit a little above the expected draw before the first power-up.

definition: A supply setting that caps the current it will deliver. If the circuit tries to draw more, the supply lowers its voltage instead, so a short shows up as a reading rather than smoke.
example: For a prototype expected to draw 40 mA, a limit of 60–80 mA is sensible.

definition: The brief surge of current a circuit draws when first powered, mostly while its capacitors charge.
A signal carried on one wire and measured against a shared ground, as opposed to a balanced (differential) signal on two wires. Both ends must share the reference.
A connection that passes a signal without a direct electrical path between the two devices' grounds, usually using an opto-isolator or transformer. DIN MIDI is the classic example in a studio.
Connecting a diode with its anode more positive than its cathode, so it can conduct once the voltage reaches its forward voltage.
Connecting a diode with its cathode more positive than its anode, so it blocks current. Every diode has a maximum reverse voltage; for LEDs it is often only a few volts.
A way of mounting components with wire leads that pass through holes in a circuit board and are soldered on the other side. Through-hole parts suit breadboards and hand soldering.

Connected end to end, one after another. For components this means one shared current path: the same current flows through each, their voltages add up to the total, and resistances in series add. For filters or processing stages it means the output of one feeds the input of the next.
example: 1 kΩ and 2.2 kΩ in series behave like one 3.2 kΩ resistor.

definition: Components connected across the same two points, so they all have the same voltage and the current splits between them. The combined resistance is always smaller than the smallest branch.
example: Two 10 kΩ resistors in parallel behave like 5 kΩ.

definition: Shorthand meaning 'in parallel with'. R1 ∥ R2 is the combined resistance of R1 and R2 connected in parallel: (R1 × R2) ÷ (R1 + R2).
example: 10 kΩ ∥ 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ.

definition: How easily current flows through something: one divided by its resistance, measured in siemens (S). Conductances in parallel simply add.
example: A 1 kΩ resistor has a conductance of 0.001 S.

definition: Whatever draws current from a circuit's output, such as an ADC input, a meter or another board. A load across a divider's bottom resistor pulls its output down.
example: A 10 kΩ load on a 10 kΩ/10 kΩ divider from 3.3 V drags it from 1.65 V to 1.1 V.

definition: The resistance a source appears to have in series with its output, which sets how much its voltage drops when loaded. For a resistive divider it is the two resistors in parallel.
example: A 10 kΩ/10 kΩ divider has an output resistance of 5 kΩ.

definition: A way of replacing any circuit of sources and resistors, as seen from two terminals, by one voltage source in series with one resistance. To find the resistance, replace ideal voltage sources with short circuits.
A circuit that holds its output voltage steady as the input voltage and the load current change. Boards use one to make 3.3 V from 5 V USB; a resistor divider can't do this job.
A voltage regulator that drops the excess voltage across a transistor as heat. It is quieter than a switch-mode regulator, so it is often used for analogue audio supplies.
The strip of resistive material inside a potentiometer that the wiper slides along. Its end-to-end resistance is the pot's marked value.

A pot whose resistance changes slowly at first then quickly, so a volume control feels even to the ear. A common specification puts the wiper at 10% of the track at mid-rotation; cheap ones approximate the curve with two linear sections.

A typical potentiometer marking: the letter is the taper code and 10K is the track resistance (10 kΩ). 'B' commonly means linear on Asian and US parts, but letter codes vary, so check the datasheet or measure at mid-rotation.
A component that can't amplify or generate power, such as a resistor, capacitor, inductor or switch.
Coloured bands that mark a through-hole resistor's value, multiplier and tolerance, defined by IEC 60062. Black to white stand for 0 to 9; gold and silver mark tolerance or a fractional multiplier.
example: Yellow-violet-red-gold is 4, 7, ×100, ±5%: 4.7 kΩ ±5%.

definition: The international standard that defines the resistor and capacitor colour code and letter-and-digit (RKM) value marking.
How far a real part's value may be from its marked value, as a percentage. A 10 kΩ ±5% resistor may be anywhere from 9.5 kΩ to 10.5 kΩ.

The preferred-value series with 24 values per decade, each about 10% above the last (10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 18, 20, 22, 24, 27, 30 …), for ±5% parts. It contains every E12 value plus one in between each pair.
A tenfold range, such as 10 to 100 Ω or 100 Hz to 1 kHz. Preferred-value series repeat the same pattern of values in every decade.
A multimeter with a numeric display. Its voltage input is high-impedance, typically around 10 MΩ on DC volts, so it barely loads most circuits.
The insulating material between a capacitor's plates. It sets how much capacitance fits in a given size and how stable it is with voltage and temperature.

Resistance times capacitance, written τ (tau), in seconds. When a capacitor charges or discharges through a resistor, it covers about 63.2% of the remaining change every τ, and is within 1% after about 5τ.
example: 10 kΩ with 100 nF gives τ = 1 ms.

definition: A curve whose rate of change is proportional to how far it still has to go, so it moves fast at first and then ever more slowly. Capacitors charging through a resistor follow one.
A small, non-polarised capacitor with a ceramic dielectric, usually built as many thin layers. 100 nF ceramics are the standard decoupling part.
A non-polarised capacitor with a plastic film dielectric. Stable and low in distortion, so it is used in audio signal paths and filters.

A compact polarised electrolytic capacitor using tantalum. Its stripe usually marks the positive lead, the opposite of aluminium electrolytics; reversed or over-stressed, it can fail short and catch fire.
A component that only works one way round, such as an LED, diode, electrolytic or tantalum capacitor, or chip. Check each one's orientation against the schematic before powering up.

A larger capacitor, typically an electrolytic of tens to hundreds of microfarads, where power enters a board. It smooths slower, larger load changes; it complements local decoupling but can't replace it.
The maximum voltage a component, typically a capacitor, is specified to withstand continuously. Choose one comfortably above the highest voltage it will see.
example: A 10 V or 16 V capacitor is a comfortable choice on a 5 V rail.

definition: Deliberately running a part below its maximum ratings, such as voltage, power or temperature, to improve reliability. Manufacturers publish derating guidance.
The loss of capacitance in Class 2 ceramic capacitors when a DC voltage is applied, which can exceed half near the rated voltage. Manufacturers publish DC-bias curves showing what remains.

Ceramic capacitor dielectrics with high capacitance per size but values that shift with temperature, voltage and age. The code describes temperature behaviour: X7R stays within ±15% from −55 to +125 °C.
Class 1 ceramic capacitors whose value barely changes with temperature or voltage. Very stable, but only available in much smaller values than Class 2 types of the same size.
A marking on small capacitors: two digits followed by the number of zeros, in picofarads.
example: 104 means 10 followed by four zeros: 100,000 pF = 100 nF.

definition: A manufacturer of LEDs and displays whose datasheets give typical and maximum forward voltages for each colour.
Datasheet stress limits beyond which a part may be permanently damaged. They are not operating conditions: the part isn't guaranteed to work there, and living near them can shorten its life.
example: The SN74HC00's absolute maximum supply is 7 V, but it is only specified to operate from 2 V to 6 V.

definition: The datasheet table of supply, input and temperature ranges within which a part is guaranteed to meet its specifications. Design inside it, with margin.
example: The SN74HC00 is specified for a 2 V to 6 V supply.

definition: A family of general-purpose 1 A silicon rectifier diodes (1N4001 to 1N4007, differing in reverse-voltage rating), often used for reverse-polarity protection.

A diode designed to carry larger currents, used to convert AC to DC (rectification) or to block reverse current. A full-wave rectifier in a mains supply draws current in peaks twice per mains cycle, which shows up as 100 Hz in UK hum.

A diode made from a metal–semiconductor junction, with a lower forward drop than a silicon diode (about 0.2–0.4 V at small currents) and fast switching. Used for low-loss protection and external input clamps.
example: The 1N5817 Schottky is specified at 0.45 V maximum at 1 A.

definition: A common 1 A Schottky rectifier diode; its datasheet gives a maximum forward voltage of 0.45 V at 1 A.
A circuit, often just a series diode in the supply line, that stops current flowing if the supply is connected backwards. A simple diode costs its forward drop.

A diode from a signal line to a supply rail that starts conducting when the signal goes beyond the rail by about a diode drop, diverting the excess current. Chips have them built in, but they are fault protection, not level shifters.
A diode across a relay or motor coil that gives the coil's current somewhere to go when it is switched off, absorbing the voltage spike that would otherwise damage the switch.
An electrically operated switch: current through a coil pulls a mechanical contact. The coil needs a flyback diode when driven from a transistor or pin circuit.
How switches are described. Poles are the separate circuits the switch controls together; throws are the positions each pole can connect to.
example: A DPDT switch switches two circuits, each between two outputs.

definition: A switch that turns one circuit on and off. Most momentary push buttons are SPST.
A switch with one common terminal that connects to either of two others, so it can route one signal to A or B.
Two SPDT switches moved together by one lever, for example to switch both channels of a stereo signal.
Two on/off switches moved together, switching two separate circuits on and off at once.
A switch that only connects while it is held, then springs back. Most front-panel buttons are momentary.
A switch that stays in the position you leave it, such as a toggle switch.

A small momentary push button with a click, common on circuit boards. The usual four-leg type has its legs internally joined in pairs, so check with a continuity test which legs the button actually switches between.
A diagram or table of what each pin of a chip or connector does. Check which side it is drawn from: the view from the front and from the solder side are mirror images.
The dot, notch, bevel, square pad or triangle that identifies pin 1 of a chip or connector. Count the other pins from it.
The common cylindrical audio plug and socket, in 3.5 mm and 6.35 mm (¼ in) sizes. Contacts are named tip, ring and sleeve from the end of the plug.
A jack plug with two contacts: the tip carries the signal and the sleeve is ground and shield. TS connections are unbalanced.
A shape feature that lets a connector fit only the correct way round. Unkeyed headers fit both ways, including the wrong one.
The printed text and outlines on a circuit board, such as reference designators and pin 1 marks.
A group of logic chips built the same way with compatible supply voltages and thresholds, such as 74HC or 74HCT.
Input/output: a pin that connects a chip to the outside world, as an input, an output or either.
A family of processor designs licensed by Arm Ltd and used in many modern 32-bit microcontrollers, including the Cortex-M7 on the Teensy 4.1.
The datasheet threshold for a logic input: V_IH(min) is the lowest voltage guaranteed to be read as a high.
example: TI's SN74HC00 at 4.5 V has V_IH(min) = 3.15 V.

definition: The datasheet threshold for a logic input: V_IL(max) is the highest voltage guaranteed to be read as a low.
example: TI's SN74HCT00 has V_IL(max) = 0.8 V.

definition: The datasheet guarantee for a logic output: V_OH(min) is the lowest voltage it produces for a high, at a stated load current.
example: TI's SN74HC00 guarantees 3.98 V at 4 mA with a 4.5 V supply.

definition: The datasheet guarantee for a logic output: V_OL(max) is the highest voltage it produces for a low, at a stated load current.

How far a driver's worst-case output sits inside the input's guaranteed region: V_OH(min) − V_IH(min) for high and V_IL(max) − V_OL(max) for low. Positive margins mean the link is guaranteed despite noise and ground offsets.
example: A 2.4 V minimum high into a 2.0 V threshold leaves a 0.4 V high margin.

definition: The voltage range between V_IL(max) and V_IH(min), where a logic input's reading is not guaranteed.
A high-speed CMOS logic family. Its input thresholds scale with the supply, so at 4.5 V the SN74HC00 (four NAND gates) only guarantees to read 3.15 V or more as high.
A CMOS logic family with TTL-compatible inputs: powered from 4.5–5.5 V it reads 2.0 V or more as high and 0.8 V or less as low. That makes it a standard way to lift 3.3 V logic up to 5 V.
The name of a chip's positive supply pin or rail on a datasheet or schematic.
The semiconductor industry standards body that publishes, among other things, standard logic-level definitions such as LVTTL.
Low-voltage TTL: the JEDEC logic-level standard for 3.3 V logic, with outputs guaranteeing at least 2.4 V high and at most 0.4 V low at a 2 mA load.
A datasheet figure describing an average part under stated conditions. Unlike min and max values it isn't guaranteed, so don't design to it.
The supply voltage, load current, temperature and so on under which a datasheet value is guaranteed. The same parameter can differ greatly under different conditions.
example: The SN74HC00's V_OH(min) is 4.4 V at 20 µA but 3.98 V at 4 mA.

definition: The datasheet section listing guaranteed minimum and maximum values, such as output voltages and input currents, under stated test conditions.
A complete circuit of many transistors on one piece of silicon, in a package with pins. Schematics label them U1, U2 or IC1.
A through-hole chip package with two parallel rows of pins, 2.54 mm apart along each row and 7.62 mm (0.3 in) between rows for narrow types. It straddles a breadboard's centre channel.
A surface-mount chip package with two rows of gull-wing leads, smaller than a DIP.
A sudden spark of static electricity, such as from a person touching a jack. It can reach thousands of volts and damage unprotected inputs.
Current forced into a chip's pin through its clamp diodes when the pin goes beyond a supply rail. Datasheets limit it; the SN74HC00 lists ±20 mA as an absolute maximum.
When a signal driven into an unpowered chip flows through its input clamp diodes into its supply rail and partly powers it. It causes strange behaviour or damage.
example: A faintly glowing power LED on a board that's switched off but still connected is a classic sign.

definition: A capacitor, typically 100 nF ceramic, placed right at a chip's supply pin to ground. It supplies the chip's fast current pulses locally, so the supply wiring's inductance doesn't make the voltage dip and ring.
example: TI recommends 0.1 µF at each V_CC pin of the SN74HC00, as close to the pin as possible.

definition: The property of a conductor or coil that opposes changes in current, measured in henries (H). Even a short wire has some, which is why decoupling capacitors must be close to their pins.
The American National Standards Institute. US-style (ANSI/IEEE) schematic symbols draw a resistor as a zigzag; IEC symbols use a rectangle.
The label that identifies each part on a schematic, parts list and board, such as R1, C3 or U2. The letter shows the type: R resistor, C capacitor, D diode, U or IC chip, J or P connector.
A set of pins that are all electrically connected. A schematic is really a list of nets; every pin on a net is at the same voltage, ignoring wire resistance.
example: +3V3, GND and ADC0 are three nets.

definition: A name attached to a wire on a schematic. Every wire with the same label is on the same net, even with no line drawn between them.
A filled dot on a schematic marking where wires connect. Wires that cross without a dot are not connected.
Chip supply pins left off a schematic drawing and connected implicitly. Check the datasheet pinout so they aren't forgotten when wiring.
One group of five holes on a breadboard (a–e or f–j in one row) joined by a spring clip underneath. Everything plugged into a strip is one node.
The gap down the middle of a breadboard separating the a–e and f–j strips. DIP chips straddle it so each pin gets its own strip.

A long strip along the edge of a breadboard, usually marked red (+) and blue or black (−), for distributing a supply. Rails on opposite sides aren't connected, and some boards split each rail halfway.
Unintended capacitance between nearby conductors, such as adjacent breadboard strips, typically a few picofarads. It matters at high frequencies and high impedances.
Software, such as git, that records every change to a set of files so you can see history and go back. Keeping wiring notes alongside code keeps them in step.
The common input on a multimeter, where the black lead stays for every measurement.
The multimeter input jack for the red lead when measuring voltage, resistance, continuity and diode test. Move the red lead back here after measuring current.

term: DC volts and AC volts (meter settings)
definition: Multimeter settings for voltage. DC volts (marked V⎓) reads steady voltages such as supply rails and logic; AC volts reads an RMS value of the alternating part and on most meters ignores any DC level.
A deliberately weak link that melts and breaks the circuit if too much current flows. A multimeter's current ranges are fused; replace a fuse only with the exact type and rating specified.
A meter feature that picks the measurement range automatically. It chooses the scale, not how the meter is connected.
A meter display, usually OL or a lone 1, meaning the value is above the selected range, or that a resistance is open circuit.
A small, precise resistor that a meter measures current through by reading the voltage across it. In current mode a meter is nearly a short circuit because of it.
The small voltage a multimeter drops across its own shunt while measuring current. It can slightly change the circuit being measured.
A multimeter setting that beeps when the resistance between the probes is below a low threshold. Use it unpowered to check wires, joints, rails and switches and to find shorts.
A multimeter setting that passes a small current and shows the forward voltage of a diode one way (about 0.5–0.7 V for silicon) and open circuit the other. It often lights an LED faintly.
Oscilloscope scale settings: V/div is how many volts each vertical grid square represents, and time/div how much time each horizontal square represents.
example: At 1 V/div, a 3.3 V logic signal spans just over three squares.

definition: The condition, a voltage level crossed on a rising or falling edge, that starts each sweep at the same point so a repeating waveform stands still on screen.
An oscilloscope probe that divides the signal by ten, giving a higher input impedance (typically around 10 MΩ) and wider bandwidth than a ×1 probe. Set the scope to match.
An oscilloscope probe that measures the voltage between two points without connecting either to earth, for measuring across a component safely.
The measurement category marked on test equipment, showing which mains environments it is built to measure safely. Low-voltage synth work doesn't need it, but mains measurement does.

A pine-resin chemical in most solder cores that cleans oxide so solder can wet the metal. The HSE says rosin flux fume is a common cause of occupational asthma, so use ventilation and fume extraction.
A fan and filter or duct that captures soldering fume at the source and removes it, rather than just stirring it around the room.
Tin-lead solder of 63% tin and 37% lead. It is eutectic, melting and solidifying at 183 °C, and flows easily, but contains lead.
An alloy mix that melts and solidifies at a single temperature, with no pasty in-between phase, so a joint is less likely to be spoilt by movement as it cools.
Solder without lead, commonly tin-silver-copper (SAC) melting around 217 °C. It needs a hotter iron and gives duller joints than 63/37.
The EU (and UK) Restriction of Hazardous Substances rules, which limit lead and other substances in electronics sold there; the reason most commercial electronics use lead-free solder.
A soldering iron that holds its tip at a set temperature. SparkFun suggests 325–375 °C as a starting range for through-hole work.
Coating a soldering iron tip (or a wire) with a thin layer of fresh solder, which protects it and improves heat transfer.
Molten solder flowing out and bonding to a metal surface rather than balling up. A good joint wets both the pad and the lead.
The copper area on a circuit board where a component lead is soldered.
The shape of solder around a joint. A good through-hole fillet is a smooth, concave cone that wets both pad and lead.
A solder joint where the pad or lead didn't get hot enough, so the solder balls up, looks dull or grainy and doesn't wet properly. It often works intermittently.
Unwanted solder joining two adjacent pads or pins, making a short. Remove it with desoldering braid or a clean tip.
A copper pad that has peeled away from the board, usually from too much heat or force.
Fine copper braid coated in flux that soaks up molten solder when heated against a joint.
A signal wire and its return twisted together. Each twist reverses the voltage induced by a magnetic field, so pickup largely cancels.

A device, usually an audio transformer in each signal line, inserted between two devices to pass the signal while breaking the ground connection between them, curing a ground loop without touching the safety earth.
Noise coupling where two circuits' return currents flow through the same piece of wire or track, so one current's voltage drop appears in the other circuit's reference.
example: 100 mA of LED current through 0.05 Ω of shared ground adds 5 mV to an audio reference.

definition: Giving each sub-circuit its own return wire to one common point, so noisy return currents never share wire with sensitive audio returns.

Pin labels for the analogue and digital ground connections of a chip such as an audio codec. They identify pin functions, not a universal rule to split grounds; connect them as the manufacturer specifies.
A large continuous copper area on a circuit board used as ground. It gives return currents a low-impedance path right under their signals, which usually keeps noise lowest.
A power supply that switches current on and off rapidly and smooths it, which is efficient but leaves ripple at its switching frequency. Most USB chargers are switch-mode.
How well a circuit, such as an op-amp, codec or regulator, keeps noise on its supply out of its output, in decibels. It typically falls as frequency rises.
A low-noise, low-distortion dual audio op-amp from Texas Instruments whose datasheet includes CMRR and PSRR versus frequency graphs.
A poisonous gas produced by burning fuel. Electric soldering irons don't produce it.
A million ohms (1 MΩ = 1,000,000 Ω). Meter and scope-probe inputs are typically around 10 MΩ, so they barely load circuits built from kilohm resistors.
example: A 1 MΩ load in parallel with 10 kΩ lowers it only to about 9.9 kΩ.

definition: An input whose thresholds match the old 5 V transistor-transistor logic (TTL) family: 2.0 V or more reads as high and 0.8 V or less as low. Because the high threshold is low, a 3.3 V output can drive it reliably.
example: The SN74HCT00 has TTL-compatible inputs when powered from 4.5–5.5 V.

definition: A low, steady tone tied to the mains supply: 50 Hz in the UK and its harmonics, often with a strong 100 Hz component from rectified power supplies. It is picked up from ground loops, magnetic fields or a poorly filtered supply.
example: 1 mA of loop current in a 0.1 Ω cable shield adds about 100 µV of hum, roughly 70 dB below a −10 dBV signal.

definition: The point in a circuit chosen as the 0 V reference that other voltages are measured against, and usually the return path for current. It need not be connected to the mains safety earth.
example: "This pin is at 3.3 V" means 3.3 V above circuit ground.

definition: The SI unit of conductance: one siemens is the conductance of a one-ohm resistor, so conductance in siemens is one divided by resistance in ohms.
example: A 1 kΩ resistor has a conductance of 0.001 S (1 millisiemens).

definition: How much electric charge a component, usually a capacitor, stores for each volt across it: C = Q / V. It is measured in farads (F); practical capacitors range from a few picofarads to thousands of microfarads.
example: A 100 nF capacitor with 5 V across it holds 0.5 µC of charge.
